extracted.intended_audience: IP professionals, policymakers, national IP offices, researchers and patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of patentability standards, procedural requirements (including PCT), and related IP-system rules (utility models, trademarks, designs, and data collection practices) as presented in WIPO's 2022 indicators report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step (non‑obviousness), and (3) be industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as the core substantive standards for patentability; national and regional patent offices decide patentability according to national law. The patent system grants exclusive rights in exchange for disclosure of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term (duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During this period the patent holder may commercially exploit the invention on an exclusive basis; duration may vary by jurisdiction but 20 years is the common term referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure obligation for patent applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public so that they may be replicated by others skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is the quid pro quo for exclusionary rights; when inventions involve biological material (microorganisms) additional deposit requirements may apply (see Budapest Treaty).

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT System procedural phases and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT application process begins with the international phase (international search and optional preliminary examination and supplementary international search) and concludes with the national phase, during which national/regional patent offices decide on patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT simplifies multiple national filings by delaying the need to file separately in each jurisdiction; however, grant decisions remain at national/regional offices and the PCT does not itself grant patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/regional legal governance of patent procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for acquiring patent rights are governed by the rules and regulations of national and regional patent offices; patent rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must file with relevant national/regional offices (or enter national phase under the PCT); substantive examination and granting criteria depend on national/regional law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model confers rights to an invention for a shorter period (typically 6–10 years) and at most offices protection is granted without substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility models (and similar short-term protections) differ from patents in term, examination rigor, and procedural requirements; they may be referred to as short‑term patents in some jurisdictions (e.g., Ireland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty requirement for microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention involves microorganisms, national laws in most countries require the applicant to deposit a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Budapest Treaty, a deposit with any IDA suffices for patent procedures in all contracting states and regional patent offices that recognize the Treaty, eliminating the need to deposit in every country. An IDA is a scientific institution (culture collection). (Report notes 48 IDAs as of Sept 2022.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark distinctiveness and scope of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another; the holder of a registered trademark has the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and can block unauthorized use or confusingly similar marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark procedures and scope are governed by national/regional law. Registered trademarks can be maintained indefinitely provided renewal fees are paid. Filing may be national/regional or via the Madrid System for international designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System filing and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System allows an applicant to submit a single international application in one language and pay a single set of fees, indicating Madrid members where protection is sought; a registration recorded in the International Register has the same effect as a registration made directly with every designated Contracting Party unless a competent authority issues a refusal within a specified time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Madrid System simplifies filings and post‑registration management (central recording of changes/renewals). Decisions to grant or refuse remain with national/regional offices. The Protocol is the sole governing treaty since Oct 2016.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial-design protectability and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs protect the ornamental or aesthetic aspects of useful articles and can be protected if they are new or original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term of protection is generally five years and may be renewed for additional five‑year periods up to a total of about 15 years in most cases. In some countries industrial designs may be protected through a design patent rather than registration; procedures are governed by national/regional law and international filings via the Hague System are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: International comparability and caveats for IP statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: IP statistics are compiled using harmonized questionnaires but national laws, regulations and statistical reporting practices may vary across jurisdictions, affecting comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data may be revised and differ from previous editions or WIPO's website. The report flags specific methodological breaks (e.g., CNIPA counting change in 2017) and notes where data are not comparable across years or offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating world totals and data‑coverage methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: World totals for applications and grants/registrations are WIPO estimates; missing data are estimated using methods such as linear extrapolation and averaging adjacent data points. When an office provides data not broken down by origin, WIPO estimates resident and non‑resident counts using historical shares recorded at that office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report lists the number of offices covered per IP type and data coverage percentages (e.g., patents: totals based on 160 offices, data available for 117 which account for 99.2% of the estimated world total). Small shares are estimated; choice of estimation method depends on the office and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO IP and publishing surveys scope and data collection practices
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO collects IP data from national/regional IP offices and other authorities via annual surveys (27 questionnaires covering patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs, plant varieties) and has a separate global publishing industry survey (scope limited to trade and educational sectors and materials issued with ISBN, DOI or other book identifier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys are available in multiple languages; WIPO validates publishing survey data via legal deposit information and cooperates with regional organizations (FEP, CERLALC) to improve coverage and reduce respondent burden. Some deposits/data are voluntary or fiscal‑year based, which is noted in the datasets.
